newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr succumbs to range trade mentality.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr succumbs to range trade mentality.

text.p: The Australian dollar subsided to a softer close Tuesday as fledgling attempts to reverse its month-old downtrend fell victim to market indifference.

Trading was dominated by continued flows out of low yielders like the yen and mark but, unlike much of last year, the U.S. dollar was the main beneficiary rather than the local unit. That reflected diverging risks over monetary policy which dealers felt would handicap the Australian currency for some time yet.
The pullback also bore out suspicions of a strangle option with strikes at US$0.7740/7840. Rumour had this expiring on Friday, so the range trading mentality could linger until then.

The bulls' cause was not helped by comments from Trade Minister Tim Fischer that the recent rate cuts would lead to a "more accurate value" for the dollar. Dealers took this to mean the government was content at the currency's fall from a six year high of US$0.8212 on December 2.
The outlook was much more mixed on the crosses where the A$ was holding firm on currencies like the yen, mark and Swiss franc which looked set to be low yielders for some time to come.
But it was not faring so well against currencies where rates looked to have bottomed or be heading higher, which included sterling and the Canadian dollar as well as the U.S. unit.

Profit-taking had pulled AUD/mark back to 1.2603/12 from 1.2644/60 late Monday, but analysts felt the German currency would continue to decline given the recent litany of warnings from the Bundesbank on the state of the economy there.

The dollar's prospects also looked bright against the Swiss franc, which was vying with the yen as the most popular carry currency, where it briefly cleared the psychologically critical 1.1000 franc barrier for the first time since March 1993.
It faded a little to 1.0979/90 in late trade but that was still its best local close since June 1992 and opened the way for a rally to 1.1500 and even 1.1900.

The expectations of low or lower rates in much of Europe had been reflected in the sudden flurry of A$ eurobond issues which had seen 12 launched so far this month, worth a total A$1.3 billion, against just two in December and three in November.
In contrast yen/A$ dual currency samurais had dwindled as narrowing yield differentials and the promise of currency gains had attracted Japanese retail investors to yen/US$ issues.

Thus while US$/yen jumped to near four-year highs atop 118.00 yen, the AUD had actually drifted off to 91.57/67 yen from a 91.79/89 close Monday. In trade weighted terms the dollar also softened to 58.6 from a previous 58.7 finish.
The attraction of A$ paper had waned in the second half of last year as Australian rates were cut by 150 basis points and speculation grew the Reserve Bank would sanction antoher easing this quarter.

That contrasted with the U.S. where the next move in rates was likely to be upwards and dealers vcould not help but note that a 0.5 point cut here and a 0.25 point Fed hike would bring Australian and U.S. rates together at 5.5 percent.
That prospect filled A$-holders with fear and should ensure caution reigns ahead of the next RBA board meeting on Feb 4 and the Fed meeting on Feb 4-5. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
